processing: A black tea with a tip content recorded at up to 5.5%; the details of its manufacture are not documented.
harvest_season: Not documented. A high tip content implies young picking, but no season is recorded for this tea.
appearance_dry: Not described in detail; a tippy black leaf, going by its recorded tip content.
appearance_liquor: Not recorded; Georgian black tea generally gives a less deeply coloured cup than Indian or Ceylon tea.
taste_profile: No tasting notes survive for this tea; good Georgian black is generally fragrant and soft rather than sharp.

brewing.notes: A guide for Georgian black tea in general, since this one is historical: it extracts quickly, and 1.5 to 2 teaspoons per cup gives a stronger cup.

vintage_note: A historical pre-revolutionary tea, with no documented current production or vintages. A modern tin using the name should be treated as a revival or borrowed name unless the seller can show otherwise.
description:
Dyadyushkin's Russian Tea was a black tea grown in Georgia before the Russian Revolution, remembered as one of the best of its time. It is a historical name more than something you can buy.

What stands out in the record is its tips: up to 5.5%. Tips were a mark of quality in Georgian tea, and this level put it ahead of ordinary Chinese teas of the day.

No tasting notes for it are known. As a general guide, good Georgian black is fragrant with a soft, unsharp taste, a lighter colour than Indian or Ceylon tea, and a fast extraction.

To get a sense of the tradition, look for a tippy black tea from a current small Georgian producer. It will not be this tea, but it is the nearest living relative.
history: The tea is documented as an example of how good Georgian tea could be by the start of the 20th century. It is credited with a gold medal at the 1899 Paris exhibition. Who Dyadyushkin was and where the tea was grown remain undocumented.
